record.title: MindEval2 reports guidance-calibration failures across mental-health support models
record.summary: An October 15 preprint introduces MindEval2, pairing psychologist-developed operational rubrics with MindSim, a longitudinal synthetic-patient simulator with cross-session memory. The authors evaluate 18 language models and report that guidance calibration—over-exploring, under-guiding or giving poorly matched advice—accounts for 60–88% of each model’s rubric findings; under-guiding rises from 12% of early replies to about 70% from turn 9 onward. The evaluation uses 50 synthetic patient profiles and a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge. It is a benchmark result, not evidence of clinical effectiveness or safety in patient care.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Mental Health Quality Rubrics, developed with PhD-level psychologists, and MindSim, a longitudinal synthetic-patient harness with memory updated between interactions. They evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight counsellor models using 50 synthetic patient profiles.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that guidance-calibration issues—over-exploring, under-guiding and giving bad advice—account for 60–88% of each counsellor model’s rubric score. Under-guiding is flagged in 12% of replies in the first two turns and about 70% from turn 9 onward. Scores are produced by a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Patient-simulator realism was assessed using 180 excerpts comprising 666 turns; annotator agreement was Krippendorff’s alpha 0.58. The paper also compares surface features with 1,584 sessions from 886 people, which are not released and are reported only in aggregate.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish clinical effectiveness, patient safety, real-world prevalence of harmful responses, or that its synthetic-patient scores predict outcomes in care settings.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent replication or alternative-judge evaluation of the 18-model benchmark findings was performed.
The simulator is synthetic and realism ratings show moderate inter-annotator agreement; alignment with diverse patient populations and longitudinal care remains uncertain.
The benchmark does not measure clinical effectiveness, patient outcomes or real-world rates of harmful guidance.

brief.importance_rationale: If the evaluation captures a meaningful deployment weakness, its guidance-calibration findings could change how high-stakes mental-health support systems are assessed. Importance reflects potential consequence in this domain; the benchmark does not establish patient outcomes or real-world error prevalence.
limitations: All model findings are benchmark results reported by the paper authors; no independent replication was performed.
The main evaluation uses synthetic patient profiles generated with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge; GPT-family results may be affected by same-family judge preference.
Human realism ratings cover 180 excerpts and 666 turns, with Krippendorff alpha 0.58; this is moderate agreement, not proof that simulated patients represent patients in care.
The real-user reference consists of 1,584 anonymized sessions from 886 people, used in aggregate and not released. It does not provide outcome labels for counsellor effectiveness or harm.
The benchmark does not establish clinical effectiveness, patient safety or real-world prevalence of harmful advice.
brief.summary: An October 15 preprint introduces MindEval2, pairing psychologist-developed operational rubrics with MindSim, a longitudinal synthetic-patient simulator with cross-session memory. The authors evaluate 18 language models and report that guidance calibration—over-exploring, under-guiding or giving poorly matched advice—accounts for 60–88% of each model’s rubric findings; under-guiding rises from 12% of early replies to about 70% from turn 9 onward. The evaluation uses 50 synthetic patient profiles and a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge. It is a benchmark result, not evidence of clinical effectiveness or safety in patient care.

technical.claimed_result: Across the 18 tested counsellor models, authors report guidance-calibration findings account for 60–88% of each model’s MHQR score. Under-guiding is flagged in 12% of replies in the first two turns and about 70% from turn 9 onward. The authors judge 61,819 counsellor replies using GPT-6.1 Sol; average rubric scores are computed over 150 patient-by-session scores.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected preprint documents the rubric, simulator, benchmark setup and author-reported findings. the research desk did not independently reproduce the evaluation or validate the rubric against patient outcomes.
technical.mechanism: Mental Health Quality Rubrics decompose response quality into operational issues across distortion reinforcement, factual/contextual fidelity, guidance calibration, boundaries and delivery. MindSim generates longitudinal synthetic-patient conversations from profiles and session scenarios; a running memory is updated between sessions and shared with the counsellor model. Patient turns are constrained through a dialogue-move tool before verbalization.
technical.regime: Benchmark uses 50 synthetic patient profiles simulated with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; session gaps, event categories and concealment schedules are fixed across counsellor models. It evaluates 18 proprietary and open-weight counsellor models over 150 patient-by-session scores. GPT-6.1 Sol is the single judge. Simulator validation includes human ratings of 180 excerpts/666 turns (Krippendorff alpha 0.58) and aggregate comparisons with 1,584 anonymized app sessions from 886 people; those real-user transcripts are not released.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares 18 models under a shared simulation and rubric protocol; no external clinical benchmark or patient-outcome baseline is used. GPT-family counsellor results may benefit from judge-family self-preference because the judge is GPT-6.1 Sol, as the authors note.

brief.title: MindEval2 reports guidance-calibration failures across mental-health support models
brief.why_it_matters: If the rubric and simulator are useful beyond the tested setup, they shift mental-health chatbot evaluation toward whether guidance is calibrated to conversational context over time, rather than only surface quality and boundary compliance. The result also identifies a failure mode across tested systems. Synthetic patients, one LLM judge and the absence of clinical outcomes limit what the scores establish.
